skills.name: Describe thermal expansion, the bimetallic strip and radiant energy converters

note.text:
Most substances expand when heated and contract when cooled: the particles vibrate more and take up more room. Gases expand most, then liquids, then solids.
Expansion is useful (a bimetallic strip, fitting a metal tyre on a wheel) and a nuisance (buckled rails, cracked pipes), so gaps are left in railway lines and rollers are put under bridges.
A bimetallic strip is two metals with different expansion joined together, usually brass and invar. When heated it bends, with the metal that expands more on the outside of the curve. It is used in fire alarms, thermostats and flashing indicators.
A radiant energy converter changes radiant energy into another form: a solar panel into electricity, a solar water heater into internal energy of water.
Unusual case: water contracts from 0 °C to 4 °C and expands again above 4 °C, so ice floats and lakes freeze from the top.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to explain thermal expansion, say which way a bimetallic strip bends and why, and name radiant energy converters.
Builds on: Lesson {6} (how heat moves) and Form Two particles and density.
Leads to: Lesson {8}, which begins waves; and the thermostats and solar devices used at home.

sections.heading: Expansion and its uses
sections.text:
Heating gives particles more energy, so they vibrate more strongly and need more room: the body expands. Cooling contracts it. For the same rise in temperature, gases expand most, then liquids, then solids.
Allowed for: gaps between railway lines, rollers under one end of a bridge, loops in overhead cables.
Put to use: a hot metal rim slips onto a wheel and grips as it cools; a tight lid is loosened by warming it.
Water is unusual: from {0} °C to {4} °C it contracts, and above {4} °C it expands. It is densest at {4} °C, so ice floats and a lake freezes from the top.

sections.heading: Bimetallic strips and converters
sections.text:
A bimetallic strip is two different metals, such as brass and invar, riveted together along their length. Brass expands much more than invar for the same rise.
When the strip is heated, the brass gets longer but cannot slide, so the strip bends with the brass on the outside of the curve. On cooling it bends the other way.
Uses: a fire alarm, where the strip bends and closes a circuit; a thermostat in an iron or a refrigerator, where it bends and breaks the circuit when hot.
A radiant energy converter changes the Sun's radiation into another form: a solar panel gives electricity, a solar water heater gives hot water.

key_words.meaning: the increase in size of a body when it is heated
two metals with different expansion joined together, which bends when heated
an alloy that expands very little when heated
a device that changes radiation into another form of energy

examples: a thermostat in an electric iron
a dull black solar water heater

mistake.wrong: on heating, a brass and invar strip bends with the invar on the outside
mistake.right: the brass goes on the outside
mistake.why: Brass expands more, so it must take the longer path, which is the outside of the curve.

worked_example.problem: A bimetallic strip of brass and invar is heated. Which way does it bend, and why?
steps: Brass expands much more than invar for the same rise in temperature.
The two metals are joined, so the brass cannot stretch away from the invar.
The longer side must take the outside of the curve.
worked_example.answer: it bends with the brass on the outside, that is towards the invar side

pick.q: Why does a metal bar get longer when it is heated?
pick.r: Its particles vibrate more strongly, so they push each other a little further apart
w: New particles are made inside the metal
The particles themselves get bigger
The metal takes in air as it warms
e: The number of particles does not change: the same particles take up more room.
A particle does not change size; the spacing between particles grows.
A solid metal bar does not take in air.
pick.y: Heating gives the particles more energy, so they vibrate more and need more room.

pick.q: Which expands most for the same rise in temperature?
pick.r: A gas
w: A solid
A liquid
They all expand by the same amount
e: A solid expands least: its particles are held tightly in place.
A liquid expands more than a solid but far less than a gas.
The three states expand by very different amounts.
pick.y: The freer the particles, the more the substance expands: gases most, then liquids, then solids.

pick.q: Why is a small gap left between lengths of railway line?
pick.r: So that the rails can get longer on a hot day without pushing on each other
w: To let rain drain away from the track
To make the ride quieter
To save the cost of steel
e: Drainage is handled by the bed under the track, not by the gaps.
The gaps make the familiar knocking sound; they do not make the ride quieter.
The saving in steel is tiny; the reason is expansion.
pick.y: Without the gap, expanding rails would push against each other and buckle.

pick.q: A tight metal lid will not turn on a glass jar. Why does holding it under hot water help?
pick.r: The metal lid expands more than the glass, so it becomes a little looser
w: The hot water makes the glass contract
The water washes away the dirt holding it
Hot metal becomes softer and bends
e: The glass is warmed too, and it expands as well, only by less.
Dirt is not usually what holds a lid; the tight fit is.
The lid does not get hot enough to soften.
pick.y: Metal expands more than glass for the same rise, so the fit between them loosens.

pick.q: A bimetallic strip of brass and invar is heated. Which way does it bend?
pick.r: Towards the invar, with the brass on the outside of the curve
w: Towards the brass, with the invar on the outside
It stays straight and just gets longer
It bends one way, then the other
e: Invar expands very little; the side that expands more must take the outside.
The two sides grow by different amounts, so the strip must bend.
It bends one way on heating and the other way on cooling, not both at once.
pick.y: Brass expands more, and the two are joined, so the brass takes the longer path round the outside.

pick.q: The same brass and invar strip is then cooled well below room temperature. Which way does it bend?
pick.r: The other way, with the invar on the outside
w: The same way as when heated
It stays bent as it was
It breaks apart
e: Cooling contracts the brass more, so the bending is reversed.
The strip returns through the straight shape and then bends the other way.
The two metals are riveted together and stay joined.
pick.y: Brass contracts more than invar, so now the brass is the shorter side and takes the inside of the curve.

pick.q: How does a bimetallic strip work in a fire alarm?
pick.r: The heat of a fire bends the strip until it touches a contact and completes the circuit
w: The strip melts and lets the current through
The strip blocks the current when it is hot
The strip rings the bell by vibrating
e: The strip does not melt; it bends while staying solid.
In an alarm the strip CLOSES the circuit; a thermostat is the one that breaks it.
The bell is rung by the circuit, not by the strip itself.
pick.y: Bending on heating closes a gap in the circuit, so the bell rings.

pick.q: How does a bimetallic strip control the temperature of an electric iron?
pick.r: When the iron gets too hot the strip bends and breaks the circuit, and it closes again as the iron cools
w: It bends and closes the circuit when the iron is hot
It melts at the chosen temperature
It measures the temperature on a dial only
e: Closing the circuit when hot would make the iron hotter still.
The strip stays solid; it bends instead of melting.
It does more than show a temperature: it switches the heater off and on.
pick.y: A thermostat uses the bending to switch the heater off when hot and on again when cool.

pick.q: Water is cooled from {8} °C to {0} °C. What happens to its volume?
pick.r: It contracts down to {4} °C, then expands from {4} °C to {0} °C
w: It contracts all the way
It expands all the way
It stays the same
e: Water is unusual: below {4} °C it expands as it cools.
From {8} °C to {4} °C it contracts in the ordinary way.
Its volume does change; water is densest at {4} °C.
pick.y: Water is densest at {4} °C, so cooling below that makes it expand again.

pick.q: At what temperature is water at its densest?
e: At {0} °C water has already expanded again and is less dense than at {4} °C.
Water is least dense as a liquid near its boiling point.
Water is ice below {0} °C, and ice is less dense than water.
pick.y: Between {0} °C and {4} °C water behaves unusually; at {4} °C its volume is smallest.

pick.q: Why does ice float on water?
pick.r: Water expands as it freezes, so ice is less dense than water
w: Ice is colder, and cold things float
Ice traps air bubbles that lift it
Ice is a solid, and solids always float on their liquids
e: Temperature alone does not decide floating; density does.
Even clear ice with no bubbles floats.
Most solids sink in their own liquid; water is the unusual one.
pick.y: The particles take up more room in ice than in water, so ice has the lower density.

pick.q: Why does a pond in a cold country freeze from the top down?
pick.r: Water at {4} °C is densest and sinks, so the coldest water stays on top and freezes there
w: The bottom of a pond is always warmer than the air
Ice forms first on the ground and floats up
Cold water is denser, so it freezes at the bottom
e: The bottom stays near {4} °C because of the unusual density of water, not because of the ground.
Ice forms at the surface, where the water is coldest.
Water below {4} °C is LESS dense, so it stays at the top.
pick.y: Water cooled below {4} °C rises to the surface, and the ice that forms floats, letting fish live below.
